questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: The osteoporosis definition combines reduced bone ___ with disrupted bone ___.
questions.exp: The page defines loss of bone strength in terms of low bone mass and impaired microarchitecture. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Assess the definition diagram: I Cortical bone loss is emphasized over trabecular loss. II Bone quantity alone fully describes bone strength.
questions.exp: The diagram gives trabecular > cortical involvement and separately includes microarchitectural quality. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: A postmenopausal woman has progressive back pain before a fragility fracture is recognized. Which distinction matches the source?
opts: Back pain is the earliest symptom; fracture is the characteristic manifestation
Fracture is always the earliest symptom; pain excludes osteoporosis
Tetany is the earliest symptom; back pain is unrelated
Bone pain requires high ALP and excludes osteoporosis
questions.exp: The clinical tree labels back pain as earliest and fracture as the characteristic symptom. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: The source's characteristic population is ___, with a quoted figure of ___.
questions.exp: The source labels postmenopausal women (40%); the figure is not defined well enough to treat as a universal prevalence estimate. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Match the following source fracture clues — 1) Commonest site named 2) Axial compression site illustrated later 3) Sensitive male fragility marker … A) Vertebral body B) Femoral neck C) Distal forearm
questions.exp: The page names femoral neck as most common, includes vertebral fractures and identifies distal forearm fracture as a sensitive male fragility marker. These source site rankings are not universal epidemiology. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among the chapter's common fragility-fracture sites?
questions.exp: The source lists femoral neck/hip, vertebral and Colles fractures, not mandibular condyle fracture. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: A woman has early menopause, smokes and exercises little. Which additional history strengthens the source's osteoporosis risk profile?
questions.exp: Low estrogen, early menopause, smoking, low activity and low Ca/vitamin-D intake are listed risk factors, alongside female sex, family history and alcohol. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Assess risk modification: I Family history and female sex are listed risks. II Alcohol exposure and low physical activity are also listed.
questions.exp: The page includes inherited/demographic and potentially modifiable exposures; they should not be treated as mutually exclusive groups. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Match the following drug-associated clues — 1) Pioglitazone 2) PPIs 3) Lithium … A) Nephrogenic DI/thyroid dysfunction B) Fluid retention/bladder-cancer warning C) Low Mg/tubulointerstitial injury
questions.exp: These are the accompanying drug notes. Pioglitazone's bladder-cancer wording reflects a risk warning rather than certainty of causation in each user. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among medication risks for osteoporosis listed on this page?
questions.exp: Teriparatide is an anabolic treatment discussed later; steroids, heparin and cyclosporine are in the risk list. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: In addition to aluminum and common anticonvulsants, excess replacement with ___ is listed as a bone-loss exposure.
questions.exp: L-thyroxine appears in the risk list; clinically the concern is excess thyroid hormone rather than appropriate replacement by itself. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
questions.q: A patient taking lithium develops high calcium with inappropriately elevated PTH. Which mechanism fits?
opts: Direct parathyroid destruction with low PTH
Renal PTH resistance with phosphate retention
questions.exp: Lithium alters CaSR signaling and can cause hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia; this page's 'hypo' wording conflicts with that mechanism. (Book p895)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Match the following secondary-cause categories — 1) Celiac disease 2) Hyperprolactinemia 3) Rheumatoid arthritis … A) Gastrointestinal B) Hypogonadal C) Rheumatologic
questions.exp: Celiac disease is the GI example, hyperprolactinemia can suppress gonadal function, and rheumatoid arthritis belongs to the rheumatologic group. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Which is the odd one out in the page's hypogonadal-state group?
questions.exp: Acromegaly is grouped under endocrine causes; the other three appear in the hypogonadal-state branch. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Match the following secondary-cause examples — 1) Ankylosing spondylitis 2) Hemochromatosis 3) Celiac disease … A) Inherited B) Gastrointestinal C) Rheumatologic
questions.exp: Ankylosing spondylitis appears with sarcoidosis and rheumatoid arthritis in the rheumatologic branch; hemochromatosis is inherited and celiac disease is gastrointestinal. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Which is not in the page's endocrine-cause branch for secondary osteoporosis?
questions.exp: Cushing disease, hyperparathyroidism, diabetes insipidus, acromegaly and thyrotoxicosis are listed; hypothyroidism is not in that branch. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Alongside Cushing disease and thyrotoxicosis, the source's endocrine list includes acromegaly and diabetes ___.
questions.exp: Diabetes insipidus is the wording printed in this particular list; this should not imply that diabetes mellitus has no skeletal effects. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Match the following secondary osteoporosis examples — 1) Homocystinuria/Marfan syndrome 2) Turner/Klinefelter syndromes 3) Sarcoidosis/rheumatoid arthritis … A) Inherited B) Rheumatologic C) Hypogonadal
questions.exp: The source groups homocystinuria/Marfan with inherited disorders, Turner/Klinefelter with hypogonadal states, and sarcoidosis/rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatologic causes. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Which diagnosis is the odd one out in the inherited-disease list on this page?
questions.exp: Celiac disease is in the GI branch; the other three are explicitly included in the inherited-disease branch. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: The investigation of choice named for osteoporosis is ___; the page additionally mentions trabecular bone score.
questions.exp: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry measures bone mineral density; trabecular bone score provides complementary texture-based information. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: A 67-year-old woman without a prior fracture asks about bone-density screening. Which source criterion supports DXA?
opts: Any age only after a hip fracture
Testing only with high serum calcium
questions.exp: The source lists women >65 and men >70, in addition to fracture and risk-based indications. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Assess the DXA indications listed: I Testing is restricted to women >65 and men >70 regardless of risk. II Younger adults with risk factors or prior fragility fractures may warrant testing.
questions.exp: The source does not restrict testing to age-based thresholds; symptoms, fracture history and younger high-risk patients also appear. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Match the following reference comparisons — 1) T-score 2) Z-score 3) Trabecular bone score … A) Age-matched reference B) Young-adult reference C) DXA image texture measure
questions.exp: T compares with young adults (25–30 years in the source), Z with an age-matched reference, and TBS reflects image texture rather than a second reference-age comparison. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Which DXA reference score is generally preferred for a 32-year-old premenopausal woman?
opts: Z-score using an unadjusted elderly reference
questions.exp: The comparison definition is useful, but the 'obsolete' label is not a valid universal statement. Z-scores remain important in appropriate age groups. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: A postmenopausal woman has a T-score of −1.8 and no fragility fracture. Which densitometric category fits?
questions.exp: A T-score between −1 and −2.5 is the low-bone-mass/osteopenia range; the diagnostic threshold for osteoporosis is ≤−2.5. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: In an appropriate adult, a T-score exactly −2.5 lies in which diagnostic category according to the table?
questions.exp: The diagnostic table uses ≤−2.5. A later treatment bullet prints <−2.5, but the boundary should not be lost when interpreting the table. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: A postmenopausal woman has T-score −2.9 and a low-trauma vertebral fracture. Which source category fits?
questions.exp: The table pairs an osteoporotic T-score with fracture for severe osteoporosis. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: In the plotted 60-year-old woman, the same BMD corresponds to T-score −2.5 but Z-score −1. Why?
opts: T-score changes only with body weight, not reference population
The young-adult reference has higher expected BMD than the age-matched reference
The two scores were measured at different serum calcium values
The Z-score is simply the negative of the T-score
questions.exp: The graph compares one BMD with different reference populations; this explains different standard-deviation distances. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: The biconcave vertebral appearance labeled on the radiograph is the ___ sign.
questions.exp: The images show compression fractures and a codfish/fish-mouth vertebra, rather than the hyperparathyroid skull or osteopetrotic patterns. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: A woman has osteopenia but a prior fragility fracture and high estimated fracture risk. Which treatment conclusion follows the source?
opts: Treatment may be indicated despite T-score above −2.5
Treatment is forbidden unless T-score falls below −3.5
A fracture invalidates the DXA result
questions.exp: The source includes osteopenia with fracture or raised FRAX risk as treatment indications, not just densitometric osteoporosis. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
questions.q: Assess FRAX: I It estimates fracture risk using clinical factors, optionally including femoral-neck BMD. II It is a quantity directly measured by the DXA machine, as the source shorthand implies.
questions.exp: FRAX is a calculated risk estimate. DXA BMD can contribute, but 'measured by DEXA' is an oversimplification. (Book p896)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among conditions the chapter associates with fish-mouth vertebrae?
questions.exp: The page names osteoporosis, osteomalacia and hyperparathyroidism for fish-mouth vertebrae. Osteopetrosis is more characteristically associated with dense bone and sandwich/bone-within-bone appearances. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Match the following supportive entries — 1) Vitamin D3 2) Calcium 3) Lifestyle … A) 800 IU/day B) Smoking cessation/increased activity C) 1200 mg/day
questions.exp: These are the source's supportive-care targets, alongside smoking cessation and more physical activity; individual intake requirements may differ. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Match the following drug mechanisms — 1) Bisphosphonates 2) Denosumab 3) Teriparatide … A) PTH-pathway bone formation B) RANKL inhibition C) Antiresorptive bone action
questions.exp: Bisphosphonates and denosumab are antiresorptive; intermittent teriparatide promotes bone formation through the PTH receptor pathway. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: The source ranks oral ___ ahead of ___ among bisphosphonates.
questions.exp: The oral-preferred branch prints alendronate > risedronate; suitability still depends on patient characteristics. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: A patient starts oral alendronate and asks how to reduce esophageal injury. Which instruction fits?
opts: Crush into calcium-fortified milk immediately after dinner
Take fasting before breakfast and remain upright for at least 30 minutes
Take after a large meal and lie flat for 30 minutes
Take at bedtime with minimal water and immediately recline
questions.exp: The source highlights esophagitis and advises an empty stomach 30 minutes before the first meal plus 30 minutes upright; use water and follow the product instructions. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: The IV zoledronate schedule printed for osteoporosis is ___.
questions.exp: The osteoporosis branch gives 5 mg IV yearly, distinct from other indications and dosing schedules. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes the usual oral and intravenous ibandronate osteoporosis regimens?
opts: 3 mg oral monthly; 150 mg IV every 3 months
150 mg oral monthly; 3 mg IV every 3 months
150 mg IV monthly; 3 mg oral every 3 months
150 mg oral weekly; 3 mg IV every month
questions.exp: The route is erroneous: 150 mg monthly is oral; the usual IV osteoporosis regimen is 3 mg every three months. Do not use the printed IV dose clinically. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Match the following bisphosphonate adverse-effect clues — 1) Exposed necrotic jaw bone 2) Collapsing glomerular lesion 3) Falling serum calcium … A) Hypocalcemia B) Collapsing FSGS C) Jaw osteonecrosis
questions.exp: The page lists jaw osteonecrosis, collapsing FSGS and hypocalcemia; nephrotoxicity is particularly relevant to certain IV exposures rather than an equal risk for every agent. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: A patient with estimated GFR 24 mL/min is being considered for a bisphosphonate. What concern follows the chapter's renal warning?
opts: The value is below the source's <30 mL/min contraindication threshold
Renal function cannot affect bisphosphonate selection
The value proves an anabolic drug is also always prohibited
A larger IV dose corrects reduced renal clearance
questions.exp: The source warns at GFR <30 mL/min; actual labeling varies by drug, with some using a 35 mL/min cutoff. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: The two subcutaneous bone-forming agents named are ___ and ___.
questions.exp: Teriparatide and abaloparatide activate the PTH receptor pathway; abaloparatide is a PTHrP analog, despite the source's shared recombinant-PTH heading. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Assess the source's treatment hierarchy: I It labels bisphosphonates first choice, teriparatide second line and denosumab third line. II That ranking is an unchanging rule for every fracture-risk group.
questions.exp: These rankings are printed, but treatment selection depends on fracture risk, renal function and contraindications; very-high-risk patients may merit initial anabolic therapy. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: A postmenopausal patient seeks therapy for severe hot flushes as well as bone loss. Which source-listed approach addresses the vasomotor indication but requires risk assessment?
opts: Raloxifene specifically to stop hot flushes
questions.exp: The page links hormone replacement to severe hot flushes and lists breast-cancer, coronary and stroke risks; suitability depends on regimen and patient profile. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among adverse effects specifically listed for hormone replacement therapy here?
questions.exp: The HRT entry names breast cancer, CHD and stroke; hypomagnesemic tetany is not in that adverse-effect list. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Assess strontium ranelate in this source: I It is described as purely antiresorptive with no bone-forming effect. II It is placed among first-choice routine therapies.
questions.exp: Those are the two source statements. This historical treatment note should not be mistaken for an endorsement to prescribe it. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: A patient requests calcitonin as the main long-term fracture-prevention drug. Which source assessment is most accurate?
opts: It is weakly antiresorptive and not recommended here
It is the strongest first-line hip-fracture preventive drug
It acts mainly by increasing RANKL signaling
It is the same anabolic pathway as teriparatide
questions.exp: The page calls calcitonin weakly antiresorptive with minimal vertebral-fracture action and does not recommend it in this hierarchy. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Match the following raloxifene concepts — 1) Breast action 2) Bone action 3) Important adverse effect … A) Thromboembolism B) Estrogen antagonism C) Estrogen agonism
questions.exp: Raloxifene is antiestrogenic in breast and estrogenic in bone; hot flushes and thromboembolism are listed adverse effects. The source's 'agonist everywhere' wording is too broad. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Evaluate: I Raloxifene can worsen hot flushes. II The source's vascular-antagonist shorthand means it protects against venous thromboembolism.
questions.exp: The adverse-effect list explicitly includes hot flushes and thromboembolism; vascular shorthand must not reverse that risk. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Match the following named drug targets — 1) Odanacatib 2) Saracatinib 3) Romosozumab … A) Tyrosine kinase B) Cathepsin K C) Sclerostin
questions.exp: The newer-drug list pairs these names with cathepsin K, tyrosine kinase and sclerostin inhibition respectively. (Book p897)

questions.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
questions.q: Assess the newer-drug list: I Odanacatib is paired with cathepsin K inhibition. II Every drug in the list is approved routine osteoporosis therapy.
questions.exp: Odanacatib development was discontinued and saracatinib is not routine approved osteoporosis therapy; the source list must be read as pharmacology, not a prescribing formulary. (Book p897)

units.title: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures
units.sec: Osteoporosis: bone strength, fractures and risk exposures · p895
units.guide: Bone strength includes quantity and microarchitecture; trabecular loss is emphasized. Know fragility-fracture sites, postmenopausal risks and medication associations. Source-specific frequency/site claims are not universal epidemiology.

units.title: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection
units.sec: Secondary causes, DXA scores and treatment selection · p896
units.guide: Map secondary causes by system, then interpret DXA against young-adult or age-matched references. T ≤−2.5 is the diagnostic threshold in appropriate adults. Z-scores remain useful; FRAX is a calculated fracture probability, not directly measured by DXA.

units.title: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy
units.sec: Osteoporosis: antiresorptive and anabolic therapy · p897
units.guide: Pair treatments with mechanisms, administration and adverse effects. Separate book-era rankings and investigational drugs from current prescribing. The ibandronate route/dose line contains a significant error and is explicitly corrected.
